body:
When adding a new torrent on Windows without pre-existing .bitfield cache, librqbit performs an initial hash check that takes ~20s and falsely reports success (or completes the check over zero-allocated buffers) instead of immediately identifying the file as missing/empty.

Root Cause:
In librqbit's Windows-specific implementation of FilesystemStorage::pread_exact (or the underlying OS read abstraction layer for seek_read), the actual number of read bytes returned by the System API is discarded:

Rust
// Conceptually equivalent to:
f.seek_read(buf, offset)?; // Returns std::io::Result<usize>, but `usize` is ignored
Ok(())
When reading an empty/sparse/pre-allocated file on Windows, seek_read returns Ok(0) (indicating EOF), but does not return an I/O Error. Because the returned byte count n is ignored, librqbit assumes buf was successfully filled with actual file data. In reality, buf remains populated with its default zeroed memory (0x00).

This causes the initial verification pass to incorrectly process zero-filled buffers as valid piece data rather than failing fast with an UnexpectedEof error.

Impact:

Performance Loss: Every newly added torrent on Windows suffers a ~20-second "fake verification" delay before downloading actually starts.

Inability to override from outside:

SessionOptions does not provide an option to skip initial hash checks for new torrents.

Custom StorageFactory implementations are rejected by rqbit's persistence engine (storages other than FilesystemStorageFactory are not supported).

Environment:

OS: Windows 10 / 11

librqbit version: 8.1.1, 9.0.0 (and current main)

Suggested Fix:
In the Windows branch of pread_exact (or wherever seek_read / read_at is wrapped for FilesystemStorage), strictly validate that the returned byte count equals the requested buffer length:

Rust
let n = f.seek_read(buf, offset)?;
if n < buf.len() {
    return Err(std::io::Error::new(
        std::io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof,
        "failed to fill whole buffer (file missing or truncated)",
    ).into());
}
Ok(())
Alternatively, use read_exact_at or ensure read_exact semantics are enforced across platform-specific storage drivers.

comments.body:
Thanks, would appreciate a pr fix. 

Suggested fix seems wrong though. I think you need to loop until the buffer is filled rather than bailing if n is small

Edit: and on zero n of course fail
Fixed in #630

title: bug(windows): FilesystemStorage::pread_exact ignores read bytes count, leading to false hash check pass on empty files

body:
Hi, would mDNS support fit with rqbit?

It could be useful for local network discovery, allowing rqbit to be discovered automatically on a LAN.

Not sure if this matches the project direction, so wanted to ask before working on it.

Thanks!

comments.body: Can you elaborate more? What's the end to end use case? Ie what exactly do you envision would discover rqbit, what software, and how will it make use of it?

Sure! Mainly it's about not having to look up the local IP of the remote machine just to open the web UI, or to access the API from other applications, like a script or a mobile app.

With mDNS, rqbit could advertise itself as something like `rqbit.local`, so the user could just open `http://rqbit.local:3030` from their laptop or phone, or use it from other apps too. It's built into macOS, iOS, most Linux distros, and Windows. No manual lookup needed, and it keeps working even if the IP changes.

Isn't the machine itself advertising mdns enough?

E.g. I visit rqbit with http://router.local:3030

It depends on the machine already having mDNS set up and running.

Not every machine advertises it by default (a minimal Linux server/VM often doesn't have Avahi installed), and it's not always stable when it does, macOS for example can auto-rename its hostname on conflicts, leaving stale records behind.

If rqbit advertised itself directly, it'd work out of the box in those cases without relying on the host's mDNS setup, and there are Rust crates for this that don't depend on Avahi.

How about conflict handling? If there's multiple rqbit instances running. 
Do these libraries you mention handle or somehow or it's a swath of custom code that needs to be written for this? 
And if they do handle it, what's the behaviour?
If they don't, this behaviour needs to be invented and specified

The libraries handle it, no custom logic needed. mdns-sd does the standard mDNS conflict resolution: it probes before claiming a name, so if `rqbit.local` is already taken it just becomes `rqbit-2.local`, `rqbit-3.local` and so on, same as Bonjour and Avahi.
Ok then the idea sounds reasonable to me, ready to take a PR provided the impl is reasonable of course

It returns `&ManagedTorrentShared`, but `output_folder` lives in its `options` field, which is `pub(crate)` (and `ManagedTorrentOptions` isn't a public type) — so external crates can't reach it through `shared()`. Only in-crate code (e.g. `api.rs`) can. Hence the dedicated getter.

comments.body: It was pretty simple with serde_bencode https://github.com/YGGverse/btracker/commit/8a110563f825af536d5e0a31149bd6fdee1ead15#diff-83507aee538f67148efdfe7450a18bb1467c12ba281f0e95bccb7e54b91c077cR185-R190

With .torrent files you need to ensure that the info dict hash doesn't change - otherwise it becomes a different torrent!
The ordering of fields might get messed up when you re-encode.

It seems this approach you've taken is flawed because it doesn't preserve the exact bytes of the info hash.
You could have done this with librqbit-bencode too, it has some tooling to work with that, but I don't think it has full decode-modify-encode loop which preserves exact bytes without slight tweaks.

Thanks for your tip!

I don't know how.. but it works, here is working example in the Yggdrasil network `http://[202:68d0:f0d5:b88d:1d1a:555e:2f6b:3148]:6969`

Maybe I need more experience or once somebody implements it for me, stupid

You are right, it will work just fine, because BEP 003 requires alphabetic order, and both serde bencode and librqbit bencode enforce that during encoding.

I was wrong - forgot that the spec requires it. And thus the libraries don't need to respect insertion order. 
It won't work only for malformed torrents which don't respect bep 3, as they will reorder fields. And malformed torrents shouldn't be a concern in general.

body:
## Summary

The desktop app does not register itself as the system handler for `magnet:` links on any OS. Clicking a magnet in a browser does nothing, basically users have to copy-paste into the Web UI. 

This was acknowledged as a valid request in #264 ("Maybe someday") but that issue was closed because it bundled two other unrelated/declined features. Opening a focused issue for tracking.

## Current behavior

- **macOS**: no `CFBundleURLTypes` in the `.app` `Info.plist`, and no `GetURL` Apple Event handler.
- **Windows**: no `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\magnet` registry entries.
- **Linux**: no `x-scheme-handler/magnet` MIME type in the `.desktop` file.

## Pointer

Tauri 2 ships [`tauri-plugin-deep-link`](https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/deep-linking/) which handles bundle/manifest declaration on all three desktop OSes and exposes a runtime callback. The backend side is already there : `POST /torrents` with the magnet as body works end-to-end.

## Workaround (macOS)

For anyone landing here via search: create a tiny AppleScript app that declares `magnet` in its `CFBundleURLTypes` and whose `on open location` `curl`s the URL to `http://127.0.0.1:3030/torrents`, then set it as default handler with `LSSetDefaultHandlerForURLScheme`. Survives rqbit updates because nothing in the rqbit bundle is touched.

## Environment

- rqbit-desktop **v9.0.0-beta.2**, macOS 15 (arm64). Same gap exists on Windows/Linux.

## Related

- Part 1 of #264 (rest declined).
- #367 (watch `.magnet` files), adjacent but different UX.
title: Register `magnet:` URL scheme handler in the Tauri desktop app

body:
To maximize bandwidth utilization across a fleet of idle servers, I am requesting a "Master-Worker" distributed architecture for rqbit, similar to PeerTube Remote Runners. Additionally, this requires an aggressive Aria2-style HTTP fallback and direct memory-to-cloud storage pipeline.
Here is the architectural breakdown of the requested features:
### 1. Master-Worker Distributed Chunking (The Orchestrator)
Currently, a single rqbit instance handles the entire swarm download. I propose a cluster mode where a Master Node delegates specific byte-ranges (mapped to exact Piece Indices) to multiple Worker Nodes.
 * **Mechanism:** The Master Node receives a magnet link and splits the workload. For example, Worker A is assigned pieces corresponding to 0MB-100MB, and Worker B is assigned 100MB-200MB.
 * **RPC Control:** Master uses the TCP socket RPC (or HTTP API) to instruct workers: AssignTorrent(info_hash, piece_range=[0, 250]).
 * **Swarm Efficiency:** This prevents workers from downloading duplicate chunks and aggregates the combined bandwidth of the entire cluster (e.g., 3 Gbps + idle nodes) for a single torrent.
### 2. Direct S3 / Cloudflare R2 Streaming Backend
To bypass local disk I/O bottlenecks and save local storage space, rqbit should implement an S3-compatible storage backend trait.
 * **Mechanism:** Instead of writing to local disk (mmap or fs), workers stream their downloaded pieces directly into an S3/R2 bucket using **AWS S3 Multipart Upload API**.
 * **Zero-Disk Impact:** Chunks are verified in memory (RAM) and immediately flushed to the Cloudflare R2 endpoint. Once all workers finish their assigned multipart uploads, the Master Node sends the CompleteMultipartUpload API call to assemble the final file in the cloud.
### 3. Aggressive HTTP/WebSeed Splitting (Aria2 Engine Logic)
If the P2P swarm is slow and the engine falls back to BEP-19 (WebSeeds) or direct HTTP sources, rqbit should employ aggressive parallel connection logic identical to aria2c.
 * **Mechanism:** Do not rely on a single HTTP request per WebSeed. The worker must split the assigned 100MB chunk into smaller blocks and open multiple concurrent HTTP Range requests against the same origin server.
 * **Aria2 Parity Parameters to Implement:**
   * max-connection-per-server=16 (Open up to 16 simultaneous TCP sockets to the same WebSeed).
   * split=16 (Divide the file/chunk into 16 parts downloaded concurrently).
   * min-split-size=1M (Only split if the remaining chunk is > 1MB).
   * file-allocation=none (Bypass pre-allocation since data is going to RAM/S3).
   * disk-cache=64M (Use a massive in-memory read/write buffer before flushing to R2).
### Expected Benefits:
 * **God-Mode Scaling:** Combines the network interfaces of N servers to download a single massive torrent in seconds.
 * **Egress Cost Optimization:** Bypasses local storage, routing data directly to S3/R2.
 * **Maximum HTTP Saturation:** Forces CDN origins (like Cloudflared R2, AWS S3, etc.) to yield maximum bandwidth via multi-threaded HTTP Range requests when P2P health is degraded.
Please let me know if there are architectural blockers to implementing the distributed piece-assignment via the ChunkTracker.
title: Feature: Distributed Master-Worker Chunk Assignment, Direct S3/R2 Streaming, and Aggressive HTTP Splitting

body:
This PR introduces native support for BEP-6 and BEP-48 into the rqbit engine, significantly optimizing swarm health telemetry, chunk acquisition, and memory allocation during peer handshakes. All implementations strictly adhere to the existing Tokio async runtime and zero-copy parsing architecture.
### 1. BEP-48: Tracker Scrape Protocol (tracker_comms)
Implemented a unified asynchronous scraping engine for both HTTP and UDP trackers to evaluate global swarm health (Seeders/Leechers) without joining the swarm.
 * **HTTP Scrape (tracker_comms_http):** * Implemented URL translation (/announce -> /scrape).
   * Percent-encoded info_hash arrays supporting up to 74 hashes per GET request.
   * Bypassed heap allocations by mapping parsed ByteBuf dictionaries directly into static [u8; 20] arrays instead of Vec<u8>.
 * **UDP Scrape (tracker_comms_udp):** * Implemented Action::Scrape (2) request packing and response unpacking.
   * Mapped 12-byte response blocks (seeders, completed, leechers) sequentially to the requested hashes.
   * Enforced strict transaction_id validation and 60-second connection_id TTL bounds.
 * **Unified API:** Exposed scrape_trackers utilizing tokio::task::JoinSet for parallel execution with a 5-second timeout and deduplication (favoring max seeder counts). Replaced blocking DNS with tokio::net::lookup_host.
### 2. BEP-6: Fast Extension (peer_binary_protocol & librqbit)
Optimized the chunk tracking state machine to eliminate TCP timeout bottlenecks and reduce Bitfield transmission overhead.
 * **Handshake Negotiation:** Set the 3rd bit of the 8th reserved byte (0x04) to signal Fast Extension support during initialization.
 * **Zero-Copy Parsing:** Added serialization/deserialization for Have All (0x0E), Have None (0x0F), Suggest Piece (0x0D), Reject Request (0x10), and Allowed Fast (0x11).
 * **Memory Optimization (Bitfield Bypass):** * Bypassed large Bitfield array allocations. Natively dispatching/handling Have None (for 0% states) and Have All (for 100% seeding).
 * **Async Churn Optimization:**
   * **Reject Request:** Bypassed the standard 10-second TCP timeout. A rejected request instantly drops the Tokio permit, unmarks the chunk in ChunkTracker, and wakes the event loop (new_pieces_notify.notify_waiters()) to instantly replenish the pipeline.
   * **Allowed Fast & Suggest Piece:** Maintained isolated per-peer sets (HashSet<u32> and LFU logic) in LivePeerState to dynamically adjust piece priority and allow requests even in Choked states.
### Constraints & Validation Checklist:
 * [x] **Zero-Copy Compliance:** No unnecessary Vec<u8> or String allocations in hot loops.
 * [x] **Non-Blocking I/O:** No blocking DNS or socket calls; fully integrated with Tokio's reactor.
 * [x] **Fallback Compatibility:** Gracefully falls back to legacy Bitfield and standard timeouts if 0x04 is absent in the peer handshake.
 * [x] **Data Safety:** RejectRequest targets specific chunks via unmark_chunk_downloaded instead of discarding entire piece buffers.
**Related Issues:** [Link any existing issues if applicable]
**Testing:** Verified via cargo test --workspace and cargo check --all-features. No data races or memory leaks detected in the chunk acquisition loop.

body:
### Use case

I'm building a folder-sync daemon (`rust-peerdup`) on top of librqbit that
needs membership-based access control: each share has a CRDT-managed member
list, and revoked members should be dropped from the swarm before metadata
exchange — not just denied content access at a higher layer. Same shape as
private trackers that want library-side auth, content-addressed networks,
or any application binding BT peer identity to an external authorization
model. I didn't see a prior issue/PR; happy to be pointed to one.

### Why a new hook
I've looked at other candidates. There's a gap for connection-level peer authentication:

- BEP-27 private flag: rqbit honors it; restricts discovery only
- Tracker passkeys: tracker-only; useless for DHT/PEX/direct dial
- MSE/PE: wire confidentiality, not auth (info_hash is public)
- BEP-10 with custom fields: what we'd actually use, but needs a hook to drop on failure
- disable_dht + curated peer list: sledgehammer; breaks legitimate joiners

### Proposed shape

A narrow public trait, called after the BT handshake (and again after the
BEP-10 extended handshake):

```rust
pub trait PeerFilter: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn check_handshake(&self, peer_id: &Id20, info_hash: &Id20)
        -> anyhow::Result<()> { Ok(()) }

    fn check_extended_handshake(
        &self,
        peer_id: &Id20,
        info_hash: &Id20,
        extended: &ExtendedHandshake<ByteBuf>,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<()> { Ok(()) }
}
```

`SessionOptions` gains `peer_filter: Option<Arc<dyn PeerFilter>>`. In
`PeerConnection::manage_peer`, call the filter after each handshake stage
and bail with the returned error. The same path the existing
`on_handshake` callback already uses to drop a connection.

### Backwards-compat

Default `None` → existing behavior unchanged. Default trait method bodies
return `Ok(())`. No peer-protocol-crate changes (`Id20` and
`ExtendedHandshake<ByteBuf>` are already public). `PeerConnectionHandler`
stays internal; this is a separate, narrower hook.

Roughly 100–200 lines plus a doc example. Happy to send the PR if you'd
take a contribution along these lines, just wanted to check direction first.

body:
rqbit should handle various forms of QoS for disk, CPU, and network to guarantee user experience under resource contention. The motivation extends from personal experience managing my own media server which is also seeded from directly.

I also note that disk I/O prioritization support is dependent on OS configuration for both Linux and Windows. I'm not sure about Linux, but Windows also automatically sets disk priority based on CPU priority unless overridden.

### User-interactive tasks should be prioritized over background downloads.

This means that any activity actively waited on by the user should be prioritized. Examples:

- User starts a copy/move operation which involves the HDD rqbit is using. Note that the copy/move operation may not necessarily be driven by rqbit. In this case, rqbit should inhibit/deprioritize background transfers on that drive so that the user operation would finish faster.
- User starts streaming media over the network from the computer rqbit is running on. rqbit should always be managing the DSCP field based on user-selected torrent/file priority, whether the packet is for controlling the connection in the bittorrent protocol or for file data, and whether the transfer is a background task (e.g. downloading files vs metadata for a magnet link).

### Setting DSCP/TOS on the socket based on operation type

Ideally, rqbit should always be setting the socket's DSCP to CS1 or LE for low or idle priority for background traffic, and CS0 otherwise (e.g. protocol-specific traffic or gathering info from magnet links). That would allow network devices to automatically prioritize rqbit's traffic accordingly.

### User-space I/O scheduler for OS-assisted per-disk congestion control

In a perfect world, we would just tell the OS that our file handles are "background priority" and the OS would completely manage the rest. Unfortunately, we have to deal with reality. I propose that rqbit should have per-disk I/O op congestion control analogous to TCP congestion control. For clarity, I would like to emphasize that this is separate from rqbit having a file/block scheduler (issue coming soon) which would also help with disk I/O performance.

|   How it benefits...	|   Disk op scheduler	|   File/block scheduler	|
|---	|---	|---	|
|   I/O throughput	|   N/A	|   Allows the OS/filesystem to cache data in memory effectively	|
|   QoS	|   Congestion control prevents downloads/seeding from starving user tasks of disk bandwidth	|   Allows user-defined priority per file, sequential-ish downloading with random-download strategies (not yet implemented), workaround systems with file number limits	|
|   Resource consumption	|   Dynamically throttle I/O ops under resource pressure like battery level, free memory, etc	|   Reduces power consumption by scheduling files/blocks based on which disk they are on, allowing disks to enter power-saving states.	|

It should be able to function without any OS-information or syscalls, but it can be aided by it.

### Links

Network
- DSCP: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiated_services#Class_Selector
- Socket TOS option: https://github.com/rust-lang/socket2/pull/224
- TCP congestion control: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCP_congestion_control

Linux
- Scheduling API manual: https://linux.die.net/man/2/sched_setscheduler
- ionice notes: https://utcc.utoronto.ca/~cks/space/blog/linux/IoniceNotesII

Windows
- EcoQoS CPU scheduling: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/performance-diagnostics/introducing-ecoqos/
- Scheduling API manual: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/quality-of-service
- Per-file I/O priority manual: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/ns-winbase-file_io_priority_hint_info
- File caching details: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20120120-00/?p=8493

- #288

body:
## Summary

I've put together a detailed low-level design for adding [BEP 52](https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0052.html) (BitTorrent v2) support to rqbit. The design follows the dual-option struct pattern from PR #72, the parallel hashing pipeline architecture from libtorrent, and rqbit's existing patterns (BufType generics, trait-based hash abstraction, zero-copy bencode).

**Full design document:** https://gist.github.com/meatsquirk/c1067570e47b4990de2542bcfff56057

## Proposed approach

- **v2-only first**, then complete hybrid support
- **Always-on** (no feature flag), with optional parameter to disable
- Merkle tree module lives in librqbit-core initially
- First PR scope: Phases 1 + 2 (parsing + merkle verification)

## Design highlights

### 4 implementation phases

| Phase | Scope | Key changes |
|-------|-------|-------------|
| 1. Core Types & Parsing | v2 structs, dual hash computation, file tree validation | librqbit-core: TorrentMetaV1Info.pieces becomes Option, new V2FileTreeNode/V2FileEntry, version detection via field presence |
| 2. Merkle Tree Verification | SHA-256 block hashing, merkle tree construction, piece verification | New merkle.rs in librqbit-core, PieceVerifier strategy enum (V1/V2/Hybrid) |
| 3. Peer Protocol Upgrade | Handshake v2 bit, hash request/reject/hashes messages | Standard protocol messages (IDs 21/22/23), NOT BEP 10 extended messages |
| 4. Torrent Creation | Dual pipeline (SHA-1 + SHA-256), file-aligned v2 pieces | Extended create_torrent with TorrentVersion enum |

### Key correctness decisions

- **Merkle padding**: all-zero hashes (32 bytes of 0x00), not hash(zeros) — per BEP 52 spec
- **Piece layer trimming**: trailing hashes covering only beyond-EOF data are omitted
- **Piece layers validation**: .torrent files must have piece layers present; each entry's merkle root is verified against pieces_root from the file tree
- **Hybrid torrents**: both v1 SHA-1 and v2 SHA-256 merkle checks must pass per piece (not "prefer v2"); metadata consistency cross-checked at load time
- **Version detection**: uses field presence (pieces blob + file_tree/meta_version), not info_hash comparison — SHA-1 is computed for all torrents as a convenience but doesn't imply v1 presence
- **Hash messages**: standard peer wire protocol messages (fixed IDs 21/22/23), not BEP 10 extended messages
- **File tree validation**: root must be directory, path traversal prevention (.././separators), raw byte-string key ordering

### Compatibility

- Zero behavioral change for existing v1 torrents
- info_hash: Id20 field and as_id20() accessor unchanged
- Breaking changes isolated to librqbit-core v6 and librqbit-peer-protocol v5 (pre-1.0 crates)

## What I'm looking for

I'd like feedback on:

1. **Overall approach** — does the dual-option struct pattern still feel right for this scope?
2. **Phase ordering** — v2-only-first vs hybrid-first
3. **Scope of first PR** — Phases 1+2 (parsing + verification) as a single PR, or split further?
4. **Any concerns** about the design before I start implementation

Happy to adjust the design based on feedback. The full document (~2000 lines) covers architecture analysis, code sketches, test strategy, migration plan, and risk register.

comments.body: Implemented this here: https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/554

If I open Claude Code and ask it to plan and implement BTv2, how will it differ from this?
I.e. what work have you actually done yourself?

Understandable -> willing to work toward a better approach here including if necessary smaller PR's if this makes it easier for you -> possibly into 4 blocks.

- PR 1: Introduce InfoHash abstraction
- PR 2: Add Merkle tree module + tests
- PR 3: Wire v2 into builder
- PR 4: BEP52 handshake logic

Fundamentally this is a code port from libtorrent and with an open spec (bep52) to assist in ensuring the accuracy of the implementation -> this is where AI shines -> replicate patterns that exist.

To answer your question, If you only did this with Claude and the prompt you provided, most likely it will: 

- It would veer from the BEP52 standard quite a bit, you need to constantly reference some source of truth in terms of documentation and steer it toward that and then test toward it. In this case i used c++ libtorrent as a reference for the logic patterns and the BEP52 documentation as a constant reference to ensure tests are accurate.
- It would implement a bunch of stubs and tests that verify the stubs. Then tell you it passes all tests and your ready to go...i did extensive review after this both vs diagrams and with gpt 5.2.
- It would fail e2e tests. 

Here were my steps:

1. Define low level design document. I created a gist (low leve design) for this. https://gist.github.com/meatsquirk/c1067570e47b4990de2542bcfff56057. The doc was based on the BEP 52 spec and a C++ libtorrent implementation of that spec.
2. I reviewed the low level design document.
3. Review code and document using GPT 5.2 (codex) with appropriate document used as context.
4. Implement each phase using claude code referencing the spec and low level design.
5. Review after each implementation phase with gpt 5.2 and test resolving issues i find during test
6. Ensure e2e tests work 
7. **Validated diagrams**, and compare diagrams vs code. I believe this is the most important part.

I'd also be willing to test the interoperability with another non-rust bit torrent client which is where these things often break.

Hey, thanks for the update,

If you could structure this into small (e.g. 500 LoC max) reviewable pieces that make sense to merge on its own, and you're willing to do due diligence in ensuring stability, performance and health of existing v1 code, then I'm good to proceed. 
It's fine if the code for some time will be in the state where v2 is partially there but not fully supported.
Let's not rush the full impl, as there might be some crucial feedback in the first portions.

Strategy - 16 PR's ~500 LOC each

- **Stacked PRs:** Each PR branches from the previous. When PR N merges to main, rebase N+1 onto main.
- **Dormant code:** V2 types and modules are added but not wired into the runtime until later PRs. No v1 behavior changes until the dispatch layer (PR 9).
- **Incremental docs:** Each PR description includes a summary of what capability it adds. No separate documentation PR — docs are updated incrementally.
- **Test coverage:** Each PR includes tests for its own changes. Existing v1 tests must pass at every step.

At the moment, as far as I can see, the client only sends the first announce request when you `unpause` (start) a torrent, and then enters a loop that sends further requests at a given interval (`min_interval` or `interval`).

First, I think the default behavior should be to send announce requests at `interval`, not `min_interval`, since many trackers return a very low `min_interval` (often around 1 minute), which is a bit overkill - especially when running several thousand torrents.

Second, the client should send announce requests with `event=completed` and `event=stopped` immediately, rather than waiting until the next scheduled interval.

Finally, when the session is being destroyed, the client should send an `event=stopped` announce for all torrents.

I’m happy to submit a PR to address these issues if you agree with the proposed behavior.

body: I haven't seen other BitTorrent clients try to integrate io_uring yet on Linux builds. Given the heavy focus on file writes and asynchronous nature of the BitTorrent protocol, it seems , at least on the surface, to be a fairly suitable option. Might be worth investigating if adding support for io_uring based read/writes would yield resource savings.

comments.body: Came across this project which seems a good highlight of how performance beneficial this could be: https://github.com/Nehliin/vortex

Implementing io_uring support in rqbit has a few fundamental challenges: for max gains, you need to design your whole app around it - selective adoption loses most of these benefits.

While `tokio-uring` exists, it's a separate runtime, not a drop-in for Tokio. You can't just mix regular Tokio async code with io_uring - you'd need to rewrite things to use its specific types. And using other io_uring crates would mean a complete rewrite - even harder.

On top of that, rqbit is cross-platform while io_uring is Linux-specific, so we'd be maintaining two code paths. It also doesn't help that Linux isn't my main dev environment - OSX is.

And honestly, for rqbit the bottleneck is usually network bandwidth or disk throughput, not syscall / context switching overhead.

The most realistic option would be a dedicated io_uring-based storage backend just for file operations on Linux (where tokio::fs isn't used for perf reasons), but the maintenance burden probably isn't worth the modest gains for this use case.

> Came across this project which seems a good highlight of how performance beneficial this could be:

While vortex is impressive, the relative perf improvement of vortex vs transmission-cli (given in their README at the time of writing this) doesn't indicate neither that vortex is 3x faster than rqbit, or that rqbit-iouring would become 3x faster than rqbit today. 

My hunch is that rqbit might become a bit faster with io_uring, but at a giant cost stemming from the reasons described above.

Alright, makes sense to me. This was mostly a passing curiosity on my end to see if there was any gains to be made here. I might spend some time benchmarking rqbit against vortex and seeing if it would be worth the effort to try to factor out some common tooling (i.e. web API surface, shared libraries, UIs) at a later point in time.

Although I agree that a bittorrent client wouldn't be bottlenecked by random I/O throughput most of the time, I still want to point out that completion-style I/O in general seems like the future. Windows has been built from the beginning on completion-style I/O, and [Tokio's `mio` has to resort to using undocumented APIs (Afd) to get readiness-style I/O at a respectable performance level](https://notgull.net/device-afd/).

I'm not sure what the story on macOS is with their version of completion-style I/O and it's definitely not a priority compared to many other things, but I would say it's still worth keeping in mind when architecting new APIs in the future.

There's a tracking issue for a `LocalWaker` which is one of the primary blockers of high-performance `Future`s on completion-style I/O runtimes. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/118959

body:
Version: [v9.0.0-beta.1](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/releases/tag/v9.0.0-beta.1)

There is an issue regarding resource leakage of FDs and the growth of RSS usage. After testing for roughly 6.5 days, the results showed:

```
5,194 open handles (via /proc/[pid]/fd)
8.6 GB of private dirty RSS (via smaps).
40 Active TCP connections (via ss), there is no way 40 connections are accessing 5,000 files.
```
Example:
```
ls -l /proc/1152589/fd | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 5
    662 [1080p].mkv
    600 [1080p].srt
    301 [redacted].mkv
    136 [redacted].mkv
     61 .flac
```

There is a leak caused by FilesystemStorage opening a file handle for every file in a torrent's metadata and not doing any pooling or LRU eviction for these later.

In this struct, during init, every file's metadata is opened and pushed into this vector. There isn't any other way to limit the current open files. This scales exponentially as you increase the number of files.

```
pub struct FilesystemStorage {
    pub(super) output_folder: PathBuf,
    pub(super) opened_files: Vec<OpenedFile>,
}
```
Also there is descriptor duplication in `take_clone` (crates/librqbit/src/storage/filesystem/opened_file.rs)
These tasks are long-lived asynchronous tasks. There is a ghost ownership where the file object is never dropped. This leads to Anonymous Memory which grows linearly.
```
  pub fn take_clone(&self) -> anyhow::Result<Self> {
      let f = std::mem::take(&mut *self.file.write());
      Ok(Self {
          file: RwLock::new(f),
      })
  }
```

comments.body:
> this scales exponentially

Didn't understand this. Yes, every file in the torrent is opened once at init and keeps being open until you pause. So if your torrent has 5000 files, then you'll have 5000 fds. 

Where's "exponentially" here?
And where's the growth over time coming from?

> there's descriptor duplication

The piece of code you referenced takes an option and leaves None in its old place. Where's duplication? The file isn't reopened.

All in all, I don't see from your comment where any leaks would be coming from. Keeping as many fds open as there's files in the torrent is just how things are done today - kind of by design, it's intentional. 

Leaking would happen if more and more fds are open over time. Is that what you observe? In that case I don't see how it would be coming from the referenced code.

> there's descriptor duplication

There is 662 handles opened for the same file, but there are not 662 files in my library. I don't have 5,000 files total, yet the app is holding 5,000+ FDs indefinitely.

The only way to run this on a server for a long period of time is to set a RAM limit and let the OS decide when to kill the process ID. Because there is no LRU or FilePool, the process just hits unbounded linear growth. This isn't great for seeding hundreds of files.

There also may be some issue elsewhere that causes the memory usage to grow indefinitely as time goes on. Is this intended, 600+ FDs opened for a single file even if they aren't being accessed? I'm not aware of any torrent protocol that requires every file to be kept open.
I'll look into it and see if I can repro. If somehow there's many duplicate fds for the same file, that's definitely not intended

> I'll look into it and see if I can repro. If somehow there's many duplicate fds for the same file, that's definitely not intended

There are a couple of issues that should be fixed:

1) There isn't a file pool; the current approach of using try_increase_nofile_limit() is sub-optimal. We need to have files requested from a pool that is also able to close the LRU FDs.

2) Resume states and re-checking: There is infrequent bit-field flushing in TorrentStateLive::on_piece_completed; it is currently only flushed every 16MB of data. There is also no flush during a pause or when the application closes/terminates. It should handle even crashing; you could easily track file completion by writing a JSON or DB file to the disk.

Also, if you create this system, the fast re-check would not need to randomly choose pieces and see if their hashes match. As long as the entire file's hash doesn't change, it shouldn't trigger a re-check at all. This would avoid the constant re-checking every time I restart/terminate the program.

> This would avoid the constant re-checking every time I restart/terminate the program.

That's what --fastresume is for. It's currently still checking some pieces just in case the file got screwed but that should be tuned down.

File pool / lru cache is an ok optimization, but open fds should be very cheap anyway, so I wouldn't consider this an urgent problem by no means. The current algorithm is simple which makes the code simple. What's the **actual** problem with having 1 fd open per file in the torrent? E.g. on OSX, 10_000 open files increase the memory of a python process by 15mb which is nothing really. On linux/rust should be smaller even. Kernel shouldn't take that much space either, a few megs probably.

The only concerning thing is your report of duplicate / ever growing fds for the same files.
It appears that this is no longer an issue in #530. I'll go ahead and mark this as resolved.

Isn't the point of grabbing this lock so that other threads won't be able write to the file at the same time? Since there can be unlimited readers, this code currently has no real effect because the `lock_read` will instantaneously return. Or am I horribly misunderstanding the code?

comments.body:
The lock is there for operations that require the file to be mutable like set_length.

Actual reading / writing is done via pwrite/pread which can run concurrently unlike write/read which modify the current offset.

All peers write to different parts of the file hence it's ok to write concurrently.

Doing so, I ran into a very frustrating issue where a simple html <video> tag should be able to stream from ex. `http://127.0.0.1:3030/torrents/1/stream/1` but fetches are rejected at a network level. 

I investigated the problem, checked for CSP problems etc but found this problem:

Which links to a reference page:

When I try to verify as they suggest if querying byte ranges 0-1 indeed returns the correct byte, the media server sends the entire file. This is the exact misconfiguration as described in the reference:

`% curl --range 0-1 http://127.0.0.1:3030/torrents/1/stream/1 -o /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100  263M    0  263M    0     0   536M      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:--  536M`

comments.body:
Thanks for the bug report, was able to repro easily.

rqbit only supports this [Range](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Range) format ```Range: <unit>=<range-start>-``` which turned out to be enough for my DLNA TVs.

It treats ```Range: <unit>=<range-start>-<range-end>``` as just ```Range: <unit>=<range-start>-<range-end>```, ignoring the end.
Can you check this branch? https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/503

Looks great. Just one thing, I am not entirely familiar with the codebase, but is it desirable to call stream seek with the range start at every get request? I am not entirely sure what the seek triggers, but I remember seeing that it might trigger some recompute in the download streams.  

Can you confirm it will not apply a stop / start effect when streaming (by re-seeking). Maybe a mechanism that only actually seeks if the range is not yet downloaded is necessary? It might not be, just checking.

Seeking is free, and it doesn't pause anything. 

If the next byte isn't downloaded yet, it will block the request until it's available.

body:
A few leaks I have noticed:

1. UDP trackers are still enabled when `--socks-url` is passed. There is no way to disable them without stripping them from magnet links and falling back to a trackers file filled with HTTP trackers only.
2. rqbit leaks the DNS resolution for HTTP trackers. This is because [reqwest does *local* DNS resolution][2] for `socks5://`. For proxied resolution, you must pass `socks5h://` or `socks4a://`. Unfortunately, [rqbit errors if passed a `socks5h` URI][1].
3. Likewise, rqbit (via reqwest) is leaking DNS resolution for downloaded torrent files and peer blocklists (for the same reason as the above issue).
4. This one is low severity, but reqwest currently has an experimental HTTP3 connector. After a quick audit of the reqwest code, it looks like there's no accounting for the proxy if HTTP3 is used (I could be wrong). In theory, an HTTPS tracker *could* be serving HTTP3 traffic (i.e. UDP traffic) which would not be proxied with reqwest in its current state. I'm not a very good rust developer so I don't know if http3 is enabled in rqbit's build of reqwest.
5. Minor: The DHT is still active when `--socks-url` is passed, but this is not as big of an issue as it can be disabled.

I'm not sure if the UDP tracker one was an intentional tradeoff: i.e. there aren't very many HTTP trackers present in magnet links. But if a user passes a proxy to an application, it's generally expected that *all* traffic will be tunneled through the proxy, even if it degrades usability (for example, firefox auto-disables HTTP3 and various WebRTC functionality if a SOCKS proxy is active).

Solutions:

1. Ignore UDP trackers if there is an active proxy (or perhaps add a flag `--disable-udp-trackers`).
2. Allow `socks5h` and `socks4a` for socks_url (or maybe even require them, lest users make a mistake).
3. Same as above.
4. Ensure reqwest is built without HTTP3 support. Never attempt to use HTTP3 on an HTTPS tracker.
5. Consider auto-disabling the DHT if a proxy is passed.

Temporary solutions (for anyone reading):

1. Strip all magnet links of all trackers. Fall back to a tracker file with HTTP trackers only.
2. Pre-resolve all domains in the trackers file to IP addresses (this may break things depending on the tracker -- the tracker might need a correct `Host` header for reverse proxying). Alternatively, write an `LD_PRELOAD` which returns no records for GAI (see below, this causes reqwest to [silently pass the hostname to the proxy][3]).
3. `LD_PRELOAD` is the only solution for this one.
4. Restricting oneself to HTTP trackers only (as opposed to HTTPS) is enough of a defense here.
5. Pass `--disable-dht`.

This `LD_PRELOAD` will cause reqwest to [pass the real hostname to the proxy][3]:

``` c
int getaddrinfo(const char *name, const char *service,
                const struct addrinfo *hints, struct addrinfo **res) {
  if (res != NULL)
    *res = NULL;
  return 0;
}
```

[1]: https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/v9.0.0-beta.1/crates/librqbit/src/stream_connect.rs#L48
[2]: https://github.com/seanmonstar/reqwest/blob/v0.12.23/src/connect.rs#L517
[3]: https://github.com/seanmonstar/reqwest/blob/v0.12.23/src/connect.rs#L1600

comments.body:
> But if a user passes a proxy to an application, it's generally expected that all traffic will be tunneled through the proxy, even if it degrades usability (for example, firefox auto-disables HTTP3 and various WebRTC functionality if a SOCKS proxy is active).

I take back what I said. BT is unusable without the proper UDP trackers and DHT. 😢

Having played around with it more, I don't think all UDP should be disabled automatically when a proxy is active. Still, I think fixing a few things by allowing `socks5h` and adding `--disable-udp-trackers` is worthwhile.

Related, I can't disable PEX without blocklisting, even that's not proxy-related: https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/issues/469
I'm running rqbit from isolated container because of that - librqbit definitively is not about the privacy (at this moment).

> librqbit definitively is not about the privacy (at this moment).

It's certainly not, this was never the goal. All privacy related features are added later due to contributors either working on them or asking for them.

If you really want it to be constrained, just run it in a netns that is limited in where and how it can connect. E.g. a netns that goes through VPN, or netns that only connects to Yggdrasil etc.

@shihiro09 

> A few leaks I have noticed

I think it's more of a documentation issue. All the "leaks" you mentioned are known - it was never stated anywhere that if you set "socks-url" then every single byte will go through it.

As you have figured out yourself, it's impossible to make it work like you want due to the nature of SOCKS proxy. It's not a VPN! It's just a TCP tunnel. So only TCP traffic can go through it, which in BT is limited to BT-TCP and HTTP trackers.

So most that can be done is README can be updated to indicate that SOCKS only proxies BT-TCP and HTTP tracker traffic, but everything else goes in plaintext. BT-TCP is the most important one though, as everything else is just metadata. So it's still useful!

The only "leak" I see here btw that should be patched - is if you set socks-url, you must disable tcp/utp listen (or rqbit should do this for you automatically).

> As you have figured out yourself, it's impossible to make it work like you want due to the nature of SOCKS proxy. It's not a VPN! It's just a TCP tunnel.

SOCKS exposes a UDP tunnel (ASSOCIATE) in addition to the TCP tunnel (CONNECT). In particular, [wireproxy][1] supports ASSOCIATE via [go-socks5][2]. I haven't seen many clients that support it, but the functionality is certainly present in various pieces of software.

> The only "leak" I see here btw that should be patched - is if you set socks-url, you must disable tcp/utp listen (or rqbit should do this for you automatically).

Not allowing for `socks5h` is a bug. Out of everything listed, it's probably the simplest to fix.

> It's certainly not, this was never the goal. All privacy related features are added later due to contributors either working on them or asking for them.

If you're opposed to SOCKS as a privacy feature, it's not clear to me why it's present in the codebase in the first place. What is the intended use case? If this is your stance, it's probably best to remove it altogether. People will get the wrong idea otherwise.

[1]: https://github.com/whyvl/wireproxy
[2]: https://github.com/things-go/go-socks5

> If you're opposed to SOCKS as a privacy feature, it's not clear to me why it's present in the codebase in the first place

That comment was about the design goals of rqbit as a whole, not about the proxy feature. I don't market rqbit as "privacy centric torrent client" or say anywhere that the socks feature will protect every byte on the network.

> What is the intended use case?

It protects BT traffic. The actual data of the torrent, which is the most sensitive part.

I'm not opposed to adding the things you ask though, don't get me wrong! I just look at them as missing features vs high severity bugs - and that's a reflection of the "rqbit design goals".

That's why  updating README and the text in --help would be the first thing to do, not DNS resolution over proxy.

These are [Tauri recommended](https://tauri.app/concept/size/#cargo-configuration) settings to optimize for size that are not already set:
```
[profile.dev]
incremental = true # Compile your binary in smaller steps.

profile.release
strip = true # Ensures debug symbols are removed.
opt-level = "s" # Prioritizes small binary size. Use `3` if you prefer speed.
codegen-units = 1 # Allows LLVM to perform better optimization.
```

Does it make sense or not, to include some or all of these?

comments.body: Why would we optimize desktop releases for size? I get stripping debug symbols, but opt-level=s?

I confess that I may not know all the implications, but if opt-level=s is basically free, then why not? I get that its probably not free in that more computing resources will go into the optimizing, but I suspect its trivial. On the otherhand, the savings might be trivial. I haven't checked. Mostly, I created this to start the discussion based on Tauri's suggestions, feel free to ignore.

opt-level=s is not free, this reduces perf in favor of size - hence the "Use `3` if you prefer speed."

I'll keep it open though as other flags might benefit

body:
## Bug Report: output_folder parameter ignored on first torrent upload

**rqbit version:** 8.1.1

**Description:**
The `output_folder` parameter in `POST /torrents` is ignored on the first upload of a torrent, but works correctly on subsequent uploads of the same torrent.

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. Upload a torrent with: `POST /torrents?output_folder=/custom/path&overwrite=true`
2. Response shows `output_folder: "/default/path"` (incorrect)
3. Delete/forget the torrent: `POST /torrents/{id}/forget`
4. Upload the same torrent again with same parameters
5. Response now shows `output_folder: "/custom/path"` (correct)

**Expected behavior:**
The `output_folder` parameter should be respected on the first upload.

**Actual behavior:**
First upload ignores `output_folder`, second upload respects it.

**Workaround:**
Upload → Forget → Upload again
title: Bug Report: output_folder parameter ignored on first torrent upload

### if you want only BitTorrent traffic going through Tor

1. StreamConnect will need to be altered to return arti_client Reader/Writer, and use that instead of direct TCP/uTP connections when Tor is enabled. This is very easy.

1. DHT must be disabled. Tor doesn't support UDP anyway so it can't be router over Tor.

body:
Hello, I'm building a `python lib` / `MCP server` for rqbit to be able to use it with AI: [here](https://github.com/philogicae/rqbit-mcp)

### **The Problem**

When adding a magnet link from certain private trackers, `rqbit` consistently fails to add the torrent. This appears to be due to these specific magnets requiring 2-3 minutes to resolve metadata and establish initial peer connections. The operation times out, and the torrent is never added to the session.

This behavior contrasts with other clients like **Transmission**, which add the torrent to the list immediately and continue to retry metadata resolution indefinitely.

### **Steps to Reproduce**

1.  Obtain a magnet link from a private tracker known to have slow metadata resolution.
2.  Attempt to add this magnet link to `rqbit`.
3.  Observe that the process times out and the torrent does not appear in the torrent list.

### **Troubleshooting Done**

To rule out environmental issues, I have:

* Verified container connectivity.
* Experimented with DHT and uTP settings.
* Added an extensive list of public trackers.

None of these steps resolved the timeout issue.

### **Proposed Solution/Feature Request**

Could a feature be implemented to **"force-add"** a magnet link, even if metadata resolution is not immediately successful?

This would allow `rqbit` to add the torrent to the list and periodically retry fetching the metadata in the background, similar to the functionality in other popular torrent clients. This would prevent timeouts from stopping the torrent addition process altogether.

Thank you for your work on this great project!

comments.body:
Do you mean the desktop app? It doesn't make sense to disable HTTP API for the server, as it's the only and primary way of talking with the server anyway.

For "rqbit download" and the new "rqbit share" it starts HTTP server in read-only mode on localhost only, I don't think it's a security issue.

> Do you mean the desktop app?

Yes. Every client has their webui disabled by default.

> For "rqbit download" and the new "rqbit share" it starts HTTP server in read-only mode on localhost only, I don't think it's a security issue.

The issue here is that browsers have generally allowed arbitrary websites to connect to services running on localhost. Mitigations include:

1. CSRF protections, CORS, etc. to prevent websites from making cross-site requests to the localhost service.
2. Authentication tokens, cookies, etc. to prevent unauthorized access in the first place.

I say "have generally allowed" because browsers are FINALLY (as of this year) very slowly changing their tune here.

There are ways to fix this, they just require careful handling of CORS, etc.

body:
Thought about the feature.

In the relatively old but powerful qBittorrent client, I can still define only one network interface and binding address for each IP protocol. What about rqbit?

Since this project is relatively new, I believe that multi-interface defining would also be useful, for example:

* [x] Mycelium
* [x] Yggdrasil
* [x] CJDNS
* [x] Some VPN 1
* [x] Some VPN 2
* [ ] Internet IPv4
* [ ] Internet IPv6

This option requires multi-network binding and the spawning of announcement threads. The subject is not trivial in the implementation also, I understand; qBittorrent can only work with one selected interface at a time. Additionally, while qBittorrent supports IPv4 and IPv6 binding (2 threads) out of the box, there is no option to define multiple (2+) external IPs. It auto-resolves only one announcement address for IPv4 and one for IPv6. If I use Internet, Yggdrasil, Mycelium, and CJDNS, it will always detect only one of them (as the IPv6) and skip announcements for the other networks.

I believe a modern client should be able to handle multiple networks. It would be a nice feature in a world where torrent usage has become restricted, and local / mesh networks could help with that. But the problem, there is too many networks, and one client. Running a new separated client process for every network is not good for performance reasons.

Thank you.

comments.body:
Multiple interfaces won't be done because:
- none of the OS APIs support binding to multiple interfaces
- this would mean that we need to have multiple sockets, one for each interface, which complicates the code a lot. In addition, every packet we send will need to be routed to the correct socket, which means we'll need to implement routing ourselves, which is TOO much to be considered

body:
I found that `rqbit` operates with Ipv4 only, at least its UDP tracker implementation.

IPv6 is future, creating this issue as the feature request.

**Some related subjects**
* https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/issues/381#issuecomment-2952742738
* https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/382

comments.body:
IPv6 is partially supported already. E.g. if you discover IPv6 peers through trackers, PEX rqbit can download from them just fine. But there's still a bunch of work to be done for full support

- [x] separate or at least make dualstack listeners for TCP/UDP IPv6
- [x] merge or clean-up UDP tracker support (branch tracker-udp-dualstack)
- [x] implement DHT IPv6

I'm not very experienced with DHT, but I saw the current implementation in libtorrent: there are two separated tables for IPv4 and IPv6, with hard-coded 2 threads management. That's because qBittorrent able to detect only one IP per protocol version (but never ygg+mycelium+cjdns+internet at same time). Yes, it can handle direct connections over a shared local IPv6 interface, but it is not adapted for multi-network announcements.

In my opinion, since librqbit is a new project, it's important to create a dynamically expandable hash table:
``` rust
enum Dht {
    Ipv4(_), // v4 supported networks array
    Ipv6(_), // v6 supported networks array
    // future protocols can be added here
}
```
* then we can deploy the new thread for every member using specified driver impl.
* the potential quanity of supported networks is infinitive - developers will be able to write the own extensions and simply announce new interfaces using common multi-network session thread interface.

I believe the future in the multi-network communication: IPv6 provides an amazing ability to build independent networks for everyone. The potential number of them is maybe similar to the current Bitcoin forks quantity.

Merged these:
- https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/392 (listen on dualstack)
- https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/393 (HTTP tracker IPv6)
- https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/394 (UDP tracker IPv6)

- https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/pull/396

With this, I consider IPv6 fully supported (minus possible newly introduced bugs) :)

My feature request is I2P support. This was recently added to libtorrent. I understand that this is probably minimum priority for this library, but I figured I would make a feature request incase for the far future or if someone is interested.

The spec for torrents over I2P is a bit different: <https://geti2p.net/en/docs/applications/bittorrent>

comments.body: You can't just use a SOCKS proxy.
[emissary](https://github.com/altonen/emissary) - Rust implementation of the I2P protocol stack

As understand, `librqbit` must support B32 addresses first. This address is returning by [special trackers](https://github.com/r4sas/opentracker-i2p) ([others](http://zzz.i2p/files/trackers.html)) instead of IP. This crate would help: https://crates.io/crates/cyphernet

Some docs for developers:
https://i2p.net/en/docs/applications/bittorrent/

I've successfully implemented bittorrent file transfer over I2P using `librqbit`. Instead of refactoring the library code, I just created local IPv4 sockets for B32 peers that received from special trackers like [opentracker-i2p](https://github.com/r4sas/opentracker-i2p), by using [yosemite](https://crates.io/crates/yosemite) crate.

It works like proxy bridge over SAM, initial implementation presented in simple [code example](https://github.com/YGGverse/btracker/blob/641bef65c556d62450415593393f2da7a816a133/crates/crawler/src/i2p.rs). This is not final version, but initial commit. But it works.

P.S. Thought I should pass an additional options for I2P mode, such as disabling DHT/LSD, limiting connections, increase timeouts, etc. Future changes could be found in this experimental [branch](https://github.com/YGGverse/btracker/tree/i2p) until merge. Hope, it could be helpful.

UPD. tested solution is now merged to the [main branch](https://github.com/YGGverse/btracker/tree/main/crates/crawler): it includes async sockets timeout and other important changes.

Sorry I think my messaging was confusing - the neighboring files being (at least partially) downloaded is intended behavior, because if you download the piece, you need to checksum it, and the piece may be spread around multiple files. This is how torrent protocol works (at least v1), and other clients do it too, including qBittorrent (though the downloaded data for those is stored in a different place). What you're noticing is multiple separate things: 1. stub files with size 0 are created. Currently they always are, cause it just makes the code simpler. If we make the code more involved we can only create files on first write attempt for example. 2. neighboring files are at least partially downloaded even if unchecked. > Once the relevant pieces are fetched are they perhaps buffered before being written to the stream/on disk

The stream is (or should be) [notified](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/torrent_state/live/mod.rs#L785) as soon as the piece it's blocked on is available.

> If so what is the buffer size and can I tweak it

The only relevant constant is how much forward from the currently streamed piece is prioritized to download. It's [set to 32MB here](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/torrent_state/streaming.rs#L27)

> Is there a way to prioritize the pieces within the range that the client specifies in their request, or rather to only download those

That's [already the case](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/torrent_state/live/mod.rs#L1215). Pieces that streams need are prioritized over others.

All that said there may be bugs of course, but last time I checked it was working perfectly. 

Is the normal download mode slow too?

It works a bit differently (and possibly slower) if you are NOT downloading the file, but only streaming it. I.e. if through "only_files" you say that you don't want any files downloaded, but you start the stream, it will only download the pieces that the stream requested (up that lookahead constant). But even that worked fine last time I checked

I appreciate the prompt response.

-                .try_steal_old_slow_piece(10.)

-                .or_else(|| self.try_steal_old_slow_piece(3.))

Hi, 

In the options you need to enable session persistence. And then choose a folder to store it (if using JSON backend). There's also a postgres backend

Let me also expand on that a bit more to ensure I answer your question better

- As long as the session is running, resuming ([unpause](https://docs.rs/librqbit/latest/librqbit/struct.Session.html#method.unpause)) and [pausing](https://docs.rs/librqbit/latest/librqbit/struct.Session.html#method.pause) can happen at any time
- If [session persistence](https://docs.rs/librqbit/latest/librqbit/struct.SessionOptions.html#structfield.persistence) is enabled, it stores state in a file or DB. Then when you initialize a session with the same persistence backend, it will pick up where it left from.
- If not using persistence, if you create a new session, and add a torrent into the same output folder as it was before, it will re-check it and then resume from where it left off. You need to set "overwrite: true" for that to work, otherwise it'll complain that it doesn't want to touch already existing files.
- To increase the speed with which it checks, you can also enable [fastresume](https://docs.rs/librqbit/latest/librqbit/struct.SessionOptions.html#structfield.fastresume). It's not default as relatively new, but I haven't ever had any issues with it, so probably we can make that default soon.

It is certainly possible, but its not how it's done right now. It should be easy to add though, just need to pass it through.

[trait BitVFactory](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/bitv_factory.rs#L4) (name stands for bitvector factory) is what creates them now. Today when persistence is disabled [it's a noop](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/session.rs#L542), otherwise it gets stored in session persistence (folder with mmaped files or postgres byte field).

I can accept a PR if you expose BitVFactory and let you override it per torrent.
Here's where it's [used right now](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/torrent_state/initializing.rs#L177).  It gets the factory from the session, but if the user passed it in you can store it per torrent in e.g. [ManagedTorrentShared](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/torrent_state/mod.rs#L187)

Hi! has been long time, and now I tried to implement this!

@ikatson I worked on this today, but has not been as easy as I thought, actually add an option to store BitVFactory is easy, update the code, where is needed, a custom function to get it from the torrent and if not exists from the session, all that fine.

The challange part seems to be add this to ```AddTorrentOptions```, to make this works, we would need to use a ```Arc<dyn BitVFactory>``` inside the options to set the custom bitv_factory, and the options needs the ```Deserialze``` which requires ```Size```, so we can't add this option easily from ```AddTorrentOptions```.

There a few options about this, I have not used Tauri, so no idea why ```AddTorrentOptions``` requires ```Deserialize```.

Options I can think:

1. Use generics, this would force to all bitv_factory be the same, I don't like this idea, is like a hard limit specially if someone wants to use the lib.
2. Do not init the bitv_factory with the options, start it as ```None``` and make a function which allow us to set a new one. This have several issues, one is that the feature will be hidden (we can't found it in the ```new``` function), also is like an anti-pattern, is not clear.

From both options I like more the second one, just because it keeps flexibility, would be ideal be able to init this using the right type, but how I don't know why ```Deserialize``` is needed nor how is used, I don't know how to make a different builder which has the right needed options.

Deserialize is used in HTTP API, it deserializes from JSON.

Can you try to use serde skip https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#skip with a default None?

I have mixed feeling, I know that should works, but is like too awful for other crates and http api..., is like we should use a generic with an enum  and request a trait in each variant, or something like that, but the actual solution also could works, maybe I'm over thinking this.

comments.body:
> that if I start a download while my VPN (for work) is enabled it will use that

binding the TCP listener to a different interface won't help here. The TCP listener is only used for incoming connections. Most of the downloads are done through **outgoing** connections.

The outgoing connections to peers are just TCP connect(addr). Also DHT sends its own UDP packets, HTTP (e.g. trackers) sends its own etc. It just uses your default gateway which happens to be your VPN. I'm not aware of socket setsockopt magic, esp. cross-platform that will give you full control of the routing.

Instead, the solution to "rqbit uses one interface, everything else uses another" should be outside of rqbit. E.g. on Linux, you can put rqbit in its own network namespace, and then configure it as you wish, including routing, tunneling through VPNs etc. You could also use policy based routing.

On other platforms smth similar might exist, although I haven't tried.

> Allow binding specific network interface

Binding the TCP listener to a different interface might be useful only if you really don't want to listen for incoming connections from those interfaces, which seems very niche unless someone gives a specific example within their network setup that makes this reasonable.

Binding a TCP listener to an interface is necessary when you don't have routing setup. In my case, I use multiple VPNs all at the same time. And anytime I need an app to use a specific VPN I just bind to the VPN itself, which saves me from having to do a bunch of complicated routing setup.

In my case, it's necessary to bind the TCP listener to the VPN to see incoming connections, If I don't do it because I don't have the routing set up on my PC, then I cannot see the incoming connections and every external app just sees the port as closed.

It is true you can use namespaces but on some configurations that can really be quite a nightmare to set up. Setting TCP listener seems to more in line work with other popular VPN solutions, such as qbittorrent. 

EDIT: Typically this socket stuff should work across unix platforms, but it seems the various implementations don't all seem to work with one another.

The things I found regarding upload/download are

- [ ] tracker_comms `tracker_comms - tracker_comms_udp.rs`
- [x] dht `dht - dht.src`
- [ ] upnp `upnp - lib.rs`
- [x] setting port for upload `librqbit - session.rs`
- [x] reqwest for download stuff/misc `librqbit - session.rs`

are there any that I am missing?
Fair enough, I read about those socket options. If your prototype works as intended I'll be fine merging this in one it's ready. Thanks

> are there any that I am missing? 

Nothing else comes to mind but if they exist we'll fix them later

> Is Node.js used during the build?

Yes, if "webui" feature is enabled. It's enabled by default for rqbit binary, but not for librqbit

to disable it, you could do the following: `cargo install rqbit --no-default-features --features rust-tls,postgres`

where `--no-default-features` disables `native-tls`, `postgres`and __`webui`__
and you can then reenable the features you like with `--features <feature1>,<feature2>,<..>`

This is split off from https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/issues/285#issuecomment-2509385742

When I try to add a magnet link for an old / low-seed count torrent, the current Upload modal requires a `ListOnly` request to complete before proceeding to the next step (file selection) of the Add Torrent workflow.
Currently, this request prevents proceeding to the next step of adding the torrent via the web interface, so certain `magnet` links cannot be added.

To address this, the `ListOnly` request should have a graceful timeout and the File Selection step should be skipped, just selecting an output destination.

title: Allow `ListOnly` request to time-out gracefully in web-ui when adding torrents

body: In the rqbit web UI, the download interface offers a destination path which defaults to the download directory. As a user, I try to keep an organization system - there is `/home/rqbit/downloads/audio` and `/home/rqbit/downloads/other` and `/home/rqbit/downloads/video`, and within these I have more subdirs for more specific filing. When adding a torrent, I may not always know the exact folder I want to put it in, but I know there is some folder and I currently need to go look up my directory structure elsewhere. I'm interested in adding support for "suggested directories" and a few other quality-of-life improvements around destinations, and wanted to check if these are worth pursuing to get them upstreamed here. I started on an implementation in [this branch](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/compare/main...scottopell:rqbit:sopell/webui-filepicker) that adds another API called `dirPreview` currently, and it returns the current destination and a few directories with it. The UI is still a bit rough so I definitely have some work to do there, and I don't love the naming `dirPreview` for the API, but wanted to check and see what appetite there is for this change.

comments.body:
Hi! Implementation aside (didn't look at it yet), I'm rather neutral to this feature due to a mix of up and downsides.

Upsides: I can imagine the UI evolving to have a directory picker. Which is nicer than typing the path. 

Downsides: 
- this adds complexity to rqbit. 
- rqbit was born as API/CLI first tool, and this feature in API is UI-only and only needs to exist there to support it

I'd imagine there must be some HTML way to add a directory picker? That would alleviate all my concerns as this will stay UI only.

> I'd imagine there must be some HTML way to add a directory picker? That would alleviate all my concerns as this will stay UI only.

I'll look into this, but my guess is that any browser-native options would only be able to work on a local filesystem, where the browser can query the FS to list paths.
I run rqbit remotely and use the web interface to access a remote machine to add/remote torrents, so all my paths are relative to the remote FS.

I have a proposal that may address your concerns of having UI-only features in the UI as well as solve a 2nd problem I'm having.
Let me briefly describe my 2nd problem -- the **"Adding an old magnet"** problem:

When I try to add a magnet link for an old / low-seed count torrent, the current usage of a `ListOnly` request to request metadata about the torrent takes forever. In my environment, I'm running via an authenticating http-proxy that has a 60s timeout (that I can't control), so when adding such torrents via the web-ui, the `ListOnly` request hits 60s and times out. So I'm not actually able to add torrents that can't be listed (via the web-ui)


So, what if, instead of making the `ListOnly` request a required UI step for adding a torrent, the torrent was added as a managed torrent up-front, and then as the user selects a destination for it, what is happening behind the scenes is a series of updates to the existing torrent's `output_folder`?

Here's a proposed workflow:

1. User clicks add-torrent button, pastes the URL and clicks "Add"
2. This sends an `AddTorrent` request **without** `ListOnly` to create a `ManagedTorrent`.
3. The response has a new field `DirPreview` in the `TorrentResponseDetails` giving "directory preview" data about the current `output_folder`.
4. As the user sets a new output directory, it interacts with a new api `POST /torrents/{id_or_infohash}/update_destination`, which can respond with a fresh `TorrentResponseDetails`


If this is interesting, I can try to start off by adding `POST /torrents/{id_or_infohash}/update_destination` in order to split up the work a bit (and get myself more familiar with the code)

> I run rqbit remotely and use the web interface to access a remote machine to add/remote torrents, so all my paths are relative to the remote FS.

Ah of course! That in itself is enough to alleviate my concerns. It's plain impossible to list dirs on the client in your case, and the case is legit. So I'm for for the original proposal conceptually.

As for the second part, by a brief look, I didn't understand this: what stops you from just updating UI to add a torrent without list only by just providing magnet+ output folder?

The only reason listOnly is there now is so that you can select the files you want. But you can do that after adding the torrent too anyway. 

Sorry if not clear I'm on phone

> As for the second part, by a brief look, I didn't understand this: what stops you from just updating UI to add a torrent without list only by just providing magnet+ output folder?

Yeah, what you suggest is probably the simplest thing to start with, I like it.
Then I separately want a way to update the destination directory in the web-ui for a torrent that is already added.

So I'll start with those two changes:
1. An alternate way in the UI to add a magnet link and output directory without waiting for `ListOnly` to return.
2. Add an api to update output folder of an existing torrent

I'll revisit this issue once I get to the UI component to "set new output dir", because I have a feeling that could be utilized in the existing AddTorrent modal and augmented to solve this current issue as well.

The first one is good, but UI alone won't be enough, you need to update the backend to allow adding torrents without waiting for them to resolve the magnet. 
Ideally, "resolving magnet" would be a new torrent state but that's too big of a refactor. Maybe spawn a tokio task to add_torrent() in this case... 

As for the second one, changing output folder on an already managed torrent sounds pretty error-prone. The only sane way to attempt it is to pause, rename every file, then unpause. You will also need to update the persistence database. But anything in this process can fail mid-way, and then the torrent will be left in a screwed up state. Cleaning up that mess will be a much bigger problem. So nasty that I'd abandon the whole idea at inception. Unless you see an easier way!

Added #286 to discuss the changes needed adding a torrent without resolving magnet to split off discussion over there.

Rename isn't something I have an urgent need for, so I'll punt on that for now, you're right, it seems like that's a fairly delicate operation and not much benefit at the moment.

title: Add usage docs

body:
#### Overview
I am interested in extending `rqbit` to support **both TCP/UDP and QUIC** as potential transport protocols. Currently, `rqbit` operates over TCP/UDP, which aligns with the standard BitTorrent protocol, but adding QUIC support could bring several benefits:
- **Improved Performance**: QUIC offers faster connection setup and built-in encryption.
- **Modern Transport Capabilities**: QUIC provides multiplexed streams and better handling of network congestion.

#### Goal
The goal is to introduce an **abstract transport layer** within `rqbit` that allows interchangeable use of TCP/UDP or QUIC. This would enable `rqbit` to operate over traditional BitTorrent networks while also providing the option for a QUIC-based setup.

#### Request for Guidance
Since I’m new to working with `rqbit`'s codebase, I’d appreciate any guidance on how to approach this. Specifically:

1. **Key Components to Modify**:
   - Which modules or files in `rqbit` are responsible for TCP/UDP handling?
   - Are there specific functions or abstractions already in place that could help with creating a transport layer?

2. **Recommended Approach for Abstraction**:
   - Should I create a trait (e.g., `Transport`) to define basic operations like `connect`, `send`, `receive`, and `close`?
   - Is there an existing pattern within `rqbit` for handling multiple protocols that could be extended to support both TCP/UDP and QUIC?

3. **Potential Challenges**:
   - Are there known issues or challenges with adapting `rqbit` for non-standard transports like QUIC?
   - Would supporting QUIC potentially interfere with the BitTorrent protocol in a way that might impact compatibility?

4. **Implementation of QUIC**:
   - For implementing the QUIC transport, would you recommend using a library like `quinn`, or are there other options that might be better suited for integration with `rqbit`?

#### Additional Context
I believe this enhancement could make `rqbit` more adaptable to modern network environments, where QUIC is becoming increasingly common. However, I’d like to ensure I follow the best approach to keep `rqbit`'s structure clean and maintainable.

body:
Hello,

I’m trying to set up a test where I can share a private file between two `rqbit` nodes running on different environments: one in a Docker container and another directly on my laptop.

#### My Setup:
1. I have a private file I want to serve from one `rqbit` instance (acting as a seeder).
2. I'm running the seeder node in a Docker container, where I've specified an `OUTPUT_FOLDER` to store the file.
3. The second `rqbit` instance, running directly on my laptop, acts as the leecher and should download this file from the seeder.

#### Questions:
1. **How do I configure `rqbit` to serve a specific file** that’s already present in the `OUTPUT_FOLDER` of the Docker container? Does `rqbit` support direct seeding from existing files, or is there a specific command needed to add the file to the session?
2. **Is there a way to ensure that the two nodes (Docker and local) can discover each other** and establish a connection? Should I use a tracker or DHT for this private test, or is there another configuration recommended for local peer discovery?

#### What I’ve Tried:
- I’ve successfully created a `.torrent` file for the private file and added it to the `rqbit` session. However, the second node (leecher) is not able to initiate the download, possibly due to connection or discovery issues.

Any guidance on how to properly configure `rqbit` to serve this file between these two nodes would be greatly appreciated!

Thank you in advance for your help!

comments.body:
In short, it's totally possible. In fact, this is what is happening in the [e2e](https://github.com/ikatson/rqbit/blob/main/crates/librqbit/src/tests/e2e.rs) test - it sets up 64 servers, and a client and ensures the client can download it.

## How to replicate in LAN without a tracker

### On the server side
1. Set up the server with a well-known port (e.g. ```rqbit --tcp-min-port 1234 server start```).
1. Add the .torrent to the session, ensure the output folder matches.
1. If the previous step was done correctly, the torrent should detect that the files are already there and will start seeding at 100%.
1. Optionally, disable dht (with --disable-dht), so that it doesn't publish your torrent in DHT.

### On the client side
```rqbit download --initial-peers SERVER_IP:1234 <.torrent file or infohash> -o client_output_folder``` or the equivalent through API. Note the "initial-peers" as the discovery mechanism.

Note: I suggest using main branch

## Note on "private" file
If the file is really "private" and should not be exposed to the outside world under any circumstances, care must be taken. You need to:
1. ensure DHT is disabled
1. tcp-listen listens on 0.0.0.0 and there's no option to change it today. So ensure that rqbit is not exposed to WAN. If you use docker, the deault (non-host) network should do the job, but expose port 1234 (in the example above) to LAN. Ensure it's not exposed to the internet.
1. disable upnp port forward

## Note on other discovery mechanisms
1. If you use public DHT as the discovery mechanism the server should have a public IP or expose itself via UpnP (and your router should have public IP for that).
4. Otherwise you can set-up a tracker in your LAN, I've never done this, not sure how to do it, but shouldn't be hard I guess.
Thanks @ikatson for the response.
